standard.title: Power and authority in Medieval Europe
standard.description: the experiences and perspectives of rulers and of subject peoples, and the interaction between power and/or authority in Medieval, Renaissance or pre-modern Europe
standard.prior_knowledge: Students explain the organisation and roles of key groups in ancient society (AC9HH7K10) and understand the feudal hierarchy from AC9HH8K02. They have not yet examined how power and authority were experienced differently by rulers and subject peoples, or how those relationships were contested and changed across the medieval and early modern period.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the experiences and perspectives of rulers and subject peoples in Medieval, Renaissance or pre-modern Europe — including how power was exercised, justified and contested — and describe how interactions between power and authority shaped political change from feudalism through to early modern political systems.

nodes.label: How power was exercised and justified
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how rulers exercised and justified their power in medieval Europe — through law, religion, punishment and symbolic authority — and describe how different groups experienced that power differently.
nodes.minimum_width: At least two ways power was exercised (e.g. law, religious authority, punishment) and one example of how different groups experienced power differently.
nodes.typical_width: The multiple instruments of medieval power — legal systems, religious sanction, military force, symbolic display — and how the experience of power varied by social group; different punishments for different groups (e.g. trial by combat for nobility, ducking stools for women) as evidence of power differentials.
wider: Examine primary sources such as Matteo Villani's diary, Boccaccio's Decameron or Ibn Khaldun's recollections to understand how the Black Death disrupted the usual exercise of power and authority
Analyse the differing levels of political involvement in city-states such as guilds in Florence and Libro d'Oro in Venice as examples of how power was distributed and contested within urban contexts
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding how power was exercised and justified is prerequisite to understanding how it was contested and reformed. Students who cannot distinguish between the mechanisms of power and the justifications for it cannot analyse political change in subsequent nodes.

response_modes.reason: Students often conflate power (the ability to act) with authority (the legitimacy to act). Make the distinction explicit and scaffold analysis of specific examples — punishments, laws, religious justifications — so students can identify both the mechanism and the justification.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two instruments through which rulers exercised power in medieval Europe and explains how they were justified
Describes how the experience of power differed for at least two social groups

nodes.label: Ruling the city-states: Italian examples
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the interactions between rulers of the Italian city-states — including Florence, Venice, Naples and the Papal States — and explain how power was negotiated and contested in these political contexts.
nodes.minimum_width: A description of how power operated in at least one Italian city-state with one example of how rulers and subjects interacted.
nodes.typical_width: Primary source analysis of interactions between rulers of the Italian city-states; the differing political arrangements (monarchy vs republic); the role of guilds and merchant classes in contesting or sharing power; the impact of the Black Death on rulers' responses to lower-class demands (e.g. King Edward III's Statute of Labourers).
wider: Examine Boccaccio's Decameron as a primary source that reveals how different social groups experienced and responded to the disruption of authority during the Black Death
Analyse how the Catasto of 1427 in Florence (introduced following the end of war with Milan) reveals the relationship between fiscal power, war and political authority in city-state governance

response_modes.reason: The Italian city-states offer meaningfully different political models (monarchy, republic, theocracy) that prevent students from generalising medieval power as uniformly feudal. Varying contexts here sharpens comparative political analysis.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The contrast between Florence as a republic and Naples as a monarchy — and the role of guilds and merchant classes in each — is rich context for developing students' understanding of how political structures shape the experience of power differently for different groups.
success_criteria: Describes how power was organised in at least one Italian city-state and identifies who held authority
Explains how at least one group (e.g. guilds, merchants, lower classes) interacted with or contested the power of rulers

nodes.label: Challenging and changing power
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how power was challenged and changed across the medieval and early modern period — including responses to crises such as the Black Death, the decline of absolutism and the development of parliaments — and describe how new ideas about authority contributed to political change.
nodes.minimum_width: At least one example of how power was challenged or changed, with an explanation of what drove that challenge.
nodes.typical_width: Multiple pathways of political change — crisis-driven (Black Death → peasant uprisings → Statute of Labourers), institutional (Magna Carta → parliamentary development → Westminster system), and ideological (Enlightenment → nationalism → decline of absolutism); how the bourgeoisie and peasant classes gained and lost power with urbanisation.
wider: Examine the role of Oliver Cromwell and the execution of Charles I in the English Civil War as a case study in how the Westminster parliamentary system developed through conflict over royal authority
Investigate the Enlightenment's ideas about human freedom and constitutional government as an ideological challenge to medieval authority structures, connecting this to modern political systems

response_modes.reason: Students need to distinguish between different mechanisms of political change — crisis, institutional reform, ideological challenge — and understand how they interact. Scaffold the reasoning so students can explain not just what changed but why and how.

success_criteria: Explains at least one way in which power was challenged or changed in the medieval or early modern period
Identifies what drove the challenge to authority — whether crisis, institutional reform or ideological change

nodes.label: Continuity and change in political authority
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the change in the role and power of monarchies in Western Europe across the period — including the decline of absolutism, the development of parliaments, and the emergence of nationalism — and evaluate what changed and what continued in political authority.
nodes.minimum_width: One example of political change across the period (e.g. Magna Carta, English Civil War, Enlightenment reforms) with an explanation of what changed and what continued.
nodes.typical_width: The arc from feudal monarchy through to early modern parliamentary systems; the changing power of the bourgeoisie and peasant classes with urbanisation; the emergence of nationalism as a new basis for political authority.
wider: Compare how rulers in France, England, Spain and Russia responded differently to new and dissenting Enlightenment ideas, showing how the same ideological challenge produced different political trajectories

Examine the features of the French Ancien Régime — increasing centralisation of power in the monarchy — as a case study in how continuity in political structures can create the conditions for revolutionary change

response_modes.reason: This node integrates understanding of how power was exercised (Node 1), contested (Node 3) and transformed across the period. Invest in helping students trace the arc from medieval feudal authority to early modern parliamentary structures as a coherent historical argument.

success_criteria: Explains at least one change in the nature of political authority across the medieval and early modern period
Uses concepts of continuity and change to describe what transformed and what persisted in how authority was organised
